items.title: Cursor SDK 1.5.0: live shell output, per-call step events, and honest usage on failed runs
items.summary: Run streams now emit a shell-tool-call-delta update with each chunk of shell stdout/stderr, so you can show live shell output instead of a dead spinner. Local runs emit one step-started and one step-completed update per model call, so you can count or time steps. Usage is now reported even for runs that are cancelled or fail mid-turn (previously silent). Also new: local.onConnectionStateChange for reconnect/connected state, a configurable sandbox binary path, and HTTP/1.1 streaming for Python local agents.
items.why: If you're building any UI on top of Cursor's agent SDK, this closes the two gaps that make that UI feel broken: no live shell output, and usage numbers that silently went missing on a crash.
items.action: If you have a Cursor SDK integration, wire up the new step-started/step-completed events to show real progress instead of a spinner -- 10 minutes to try against an existing run.

eval.reason: Genuine new SDK capability (live shell streaming, step events, usage-on-failure); not a duplicate -- Claude Code's recent MCP-skills release is a different product.

items.title: Agent = Model + Harness: a concrete deterministic-gate pattern for content/agent pipelines
items.summary: Basia Kubicka rebuilt her LinkedIn content agent after discovering its "MANDATORY. NEVER SKIP." prompt instructions could report "all checks pass" without actually running the checks. Her fix: a recorded state machine (idea -> accepted -> researched -> drafted -> ready -> shipped -> measured) where a linter, a hook-length check, and a grading model all have to report in before a draft can move to "ready" -- anything deterministic moved out of the prompt and into code.
items.why: The exact failure she hit -- a prompt-only check that can silently not run and still claim success -- is the most common silent bug in home-built agent harnesses, and her fix (code-enforced gates, judgment-only LLM calls) is a pattern you can lift directly.
items.action: Audit your own harness for one check that still lives only in prompt instructions rather than code -- that's the one most likely to silently stop firing.

eval.reason: Concrete, specific technique (code-enforced state machine gates) with a real failure story behind it, not generic advice; checked against recent days, no duplicate.

items.title: Turning a single Claude Code session log into a queryable knowledge graph with Relate
items.summary: Panos Kostakos took one 26-turn, 62-tool-call Claude Code session and loaded it into Relate (an open-source embedded graph database): turns and tool calls as the episodic layer, with topics/decisions/questions tagged by the model as a semantic layer on top. He notes the approach scales to linking many sessions into one global graph, and that the topic/decision tags are the model's interpretation, not ground truth.
items.why: This is a working, minimal version of exactly the kind of episodic-plus-semantic structure that turns agent session logs into something queryable instead of a pile of transcripts -- directly adjacent to building a semantic knowledge graph over a codebase.
items.action: Try the same turn-by-turn-into-a-graph approach on one of your own Claude Code session logs as a one-evening spike, before deciding whether it's worth building into your research tooling.

items.title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: spend now tracked by PR outcome, not just tokens
items.summary: New public-beta dashboard in LangSmith links coding-agent spend (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot in VS Code, Deep Agents) directly to the GitHub PR or GitLab MR it produced, breaking spend down by PR state (open/closed/merged) and work type, with unattributed spend tracked separately. LangChain's own motivating example is their internal coding agent, Robin, where spend "started climbing" with no way to see what it was buying.
items.why: Token spend alone tells you nothing about whether an agent is earning its cost -- this is the first mainstream tool that ties the dollar number to a merged-or-not outcome.
items.action: If your team is running Claude Code or Cursor at any scale, this is worth a look specifically for the "cost per merged PR" cut, which is the number that actually matters to a budget conversation.

items.title: Building Agent Harnesses with Jev: Where Decision Models Fit -- Sydney Runkle, LangChain
items.summary: Sydney Runkle walks through where small, fast decision models like TypeSafe AI's Jev fit in an agent harness -- the layer around the core loop where extra LLM calls quietly add latency. In a LangChain A/B test, routed threads took longer than unrouted ones because of the routing LLM call itself, not the work it routed to; swapping in Jev fixed it. Comments add real detail: one names it as the classical-ML "cheap by default, escalate by exception" cascade pattern, another frames every harness decision as a cost-benefit question against a plain rule.
items.why: A concrete, measured example of a harness decision (which model routes what) quietly becoming the bottleneck -- and a specific fix, not just the general advice to "use a smaller model somewhere."
